stops.teaser: A white iron fountain that turns green every St. Patrick's Day.

stops.clue: Find the big park at the south end of the historic district and head for the large white fountain in the middle.

story: Forsyth Park began in the 1840s on 10 acres given by William Brown Hodgson. It was expanded and named for Georgia Governor John Forsyth in 1851. It covers 30 acres.
The fountain was installed in 1858 and cast by Janes, Beebe & Company. Its design comes from the work of French sculptor Michel Lienard and resembles fountains at the Place de la Concorde in Paris.

The Confederate Memorial was unveiled in 1874 and a bronze soldier was added in 1879. The Fragrant Garden was designed for the blind, and the fountain is ceremonially turned green for St. Patrick's Day.
stops.fact: The fountain is turned green for St. Patrick's Day.
stops.disputed: Many sources say Forsyth donated the land. Wikipedia says William Brown Hodgson gave the first 10 acres.

claims.t: The Forsyth Park fountain was installed in 1858.
Governor Forsyth donated the first 10 acres.
claims.why: William Brown Hodgson donated the first 10 acres.

spot.q: The fountain in the 1870 stereoview was installed in 1858, and the Confederate Memorial was unveiled in 1874. How many years later was the memorial?

story: River Street is about 2 miles long along the Savannah River, according to Wikipedia. The south side has rows of former cotton warehouses, some dating from the 1850s.

Factors Walk is built on the middle level of the sloping bluff, with warehouses beneath and Bay Street above. Cotton brokers, called factors, bargained there. The name Factors Row preserves the industry's name.
The pavement is Belgian block with streetcar tracks set in. Large tankers and container ships heading to and from the Port of Savannah sometimes pass within yards of the promenade.
stops.fact: The warehouses were built for the cotton trade.
stops.disputed: A popular claim says the cobblestones are old ship ballast stones. Wikipedia describes Belgian block paving instead.

claims.why: Wikipedia: terraces of former King Cotton warehouses.

claims.t: The paving is all old ship ballast.
claims.why: A popular story, but Wikipedia describes Belgian block paving.

spot.why: Factors Walk is built on the middle level of the sloping bluff, with warehouses beneath and Bay Street above.

story: The parish started in 1799. The present cathedral was dedicated on April 30, 1876, and Ephraim Francis Baldwin was its architect, in Gothic Revival style.
A fire destroyed the interior on February 6, 1898. The first Mass in the rebuilt building was held in December 1899, and it was rededicated on October 28, 1900.
It is 214 feet tall overall and has 81 stained-glass windows. Windows installed in 1904 came from Austria-Hungary. Pope Francis made it a minor basilica in January 2020.
stops.fact: It became a minor basilica in 2020.
stops.disputed: Older guides say the basilica title dates to the 1990s. Wikipedia says January 2020.

claims.t: The cathedral was named a basilica in 1996.
claims.why: Pope Francis elevated it in January 2020.

spot.q: A fire destroyed the cathedral's interior after it was dedicated in 1876. In what year did that fire happen?
spot.why: The fire on February 6, 1898 destroyed the interior, and it was rededicated in 1900.

stops.name: Fort Pulaski
stops.teaser: A fort with 11-foot walls that fell in 30 hours.
stops.map: Fort Pulaski National Monument, Cockspur Island, GA
stops.clue: Drive east of Savannah toward Tybee Island to Cockspur Island and find the brick fort surrounded by a moat.
stops.safety: It is a national park site on an island. Watch for traffic on the highway, stay on trails and bring water and sun protection.

q.hint: Their barrels had spiral grooves inside.
q.verify: Wikipedia and the Georgia Encyclopedia both say Union rifled cannon breached the wall. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.line: The damaged corner wall after the 1862 siege.

now.head: Today
now.label: The fort today
now.line: The brick fort sits on Cockspur Island.

story: Fort Pulaski was built from 1829 to 1847 on Cockspur Island at the mouth of the Savannah River. It was named in 1833 for Casimir Pulaski, a Polish-born soldier who fought in the American Revolution. About 25 million bricks went into it, supported by wooden pilings sunk up to 70 feet.
As a young second lieutenant, Robert E. Lee worked on its construction under Major Samuel Babcock. Sources disagree on how thick the walls were, from about 7½ to 11 feet.

In April 1862, Union forces used 36 guns, including James rifled cannons and Parrott rifles, to breach the corner wall within about 30 hours. Colonel Charles H. Olmstead surrendered reluctantly. Only two soldiers were killed. The success of rifled cannon rendered brick forts obsolete. It became a national monument on October 15, 1924.
stops.fact: Only two soldiers were killed in the siege.
stops.disputed: Dates for the surrender differ slightly. The siege began on April 10, 1862, and a photo of the surrender room is dated April 11.

claims.t: Fort Pulaski was breached by rifled cannon in 1862.
claims.why: Wikipedia: the corner wall was breached within 30 hours.

claims.t: Robert E. Lee designed Fort Pulaski.
claims.why: He worked on construction as a young lieutenant, but did not design it.

spot.q: The 1862 photo shows the fort's damaged corner wall. About how long did the Union guns take to breach it?
spot.why: Union forces breached the corner wall within about 30 hours.
